hardening.label: ASLR (DYNAMIC_BASE)
hardening.detail: DYNAMIC_BASE is not set; the image always loads at its preferred base address

hardening.label: High-entropy ASLR (HIGH_ENTROPY_VA)

hardening.label: DEP (NX_COMPAT)
hardening.detail: NX_COMPAT is set; the image opts in to data execution prevention

hardening.label: Safe exception handling (SafeSEH / NO_SEH)
hardening.detail: SafeSEH and NO_SEH apply to x86 images only

findings.title: Imports cover the full process-injection chain (allocate, write, execute)
evidence: allocate or map memory in another process: KERNEL32.dll!VirtualAllocEx
start or hijack a thread there: KERNEL32.dll!CreateRemoteThread
code: 4 call sites in .text (see the code blocks)

code.title: call to KERNEL32.dll!VirtualAllocEx in .text
limitations: x86-64 code decoded as a linear sweep (ARM64 and other instruction sets are not supported): data inside a code section can be read as instructions, and one wrong byte shifts what follows.
Only calls through the import table and import thunks are found: functions resolved at run time are invisible, and packed or protected code hides its real calls.
A view of the code, not a decompiler, an emulator or a verdict: nothing was executed, and the code shows what is called, not why.

findings.title: AWS access key ID embedded in the file

code.title: Bytes around the AWS access key ID at file offset 0xf5e (value masked)
limitations: A raw window over the file: the bytes are shown as stored, 16 to a row, and nothing says that any code uses them.
The bytes of credential-like values are replaced by 2a (an asterisk) in the hex and ASCII columns, so the values cannot be recovered from this view.
Pattern match only: the credential was not validated and may be a placeholder, documentation example, test fixture or an already revoked key.
Values are redacted in every output: only the first four characters and the length are kept.
The string list is truncated, so further secrets may exist beyond the ones listed.

findings.title: ASLR is disabled (image has a fixed base address)
evidence: ASLR (DYNAMIC_BASE): DYNAMIC_BASE is not set; the image always loads at its preferred base address
limitations: Describes how hard the file is to exploit, not whether it is malicious: older toolchains, statically linked and embedded software often lack these mitigations.
The dynamic-base flag is necessary but not sufficient: ASLR is only effective when relocation data is present.

findings.title: Embedded command lines with download, encoding or hidden-execution patterns

code.title: Bytes around 2 command lines, the first at file offset 0xe63
limitations: A raw window over the file: the bytes are shown as stored, 16 to a row, and nothing says that any code uses them.
Command lines in a binary may belong to installers, update scripts, help text or documentation rather than code that runs; they are not executed here.
Only the strings kept in the report were examined (see strings.truncated).

findings.title: Executable section with very high entropy (possible packing or encryption)
evidence: .packed: entropy 7.98, raw size 8.0 KiB, flags R-X
limitations: Compressed or encrypted resources, embedded images, archives and fonts are legitimately high-entropy; high entropy suggests packing or encryption but does not prove either.
Entropy is computed over the raw bytes of each section; very large sections are sampled.

findings.title: Section names match a known packer or protector
limitations: Section names are chosen by the linker or packer and are trivial to fake or rename.
Commercial protectors are also used on legitimate software (licensing, anti-tamper).

findings.title: Section is both writable and executable
limitations: Describes the file layout, not run-time behaviour. Packers, self-extractors, JIT-style loaders and some legacy toolchains legitimately use RWX sections.
The section flags come from the header and may not match the protection the loader finally applies.

findings.title: Hard-coded network indicators

code.title: Bytes around 3 strings (URL, IP address), the first at file offset 0xe00
limitations: A raw window over the file: the bytes are shown as stored, 16 to a row, and nothing says that any code uses them.
A string in a binary may be dead code, a library default, a documentation or licence link, an XML namespace or a decoy; presence does not show that the program contacts it.
Dotted-quad strings can be version numbers rather than IP addresses.
Strings longer than 400 characters are ignored here: concatenated string tables (Go, Rust) produce accidental matches.
Only the strings kept in the report were examined (see strings.truncated).

findings.title: Registry paths associated with autostart or hijacking

code.title: Bytes around the registry path at file offset 0xec2
limitations: A raw window over the file: the bytes are shown as stored, 16 to a row, and nothing says that any code uses them.
Installers, updaters and system utilities legitimately reference the same keys; the strings do not show the program writes them.

findings.title: Debug (PDB) path is embedded in the binary
limitations: A PDB path can reveal the build machine's directory layout, user name or project names; it is also a useful attribution and clustering hint.
The path is metadata written by the linker and can be edited or stripped without changing behaviour.

findings.title: No embedded code signature present
evidence: Authenticode signature present (not verified): no Authenticode certificate table
limitations: Windows system files and driver packages are often signed through security catalogs (.cat) instead of an embedded signature, which this check cannot see.
Only the presence of a signature is checked; a present signature is not verified here and an absent one is normal for open-source and internal tools.

findings.title: Sections with unusual structure
evidence: .packed: section name is typical of an unnamed packer (.packed)
.rwx: writable and executable (RWX); unusual section name ".rwx"
limitations: Odd section names and sizes are produced by many legitimate toolchains (Go, Delphi, custom linkers, resource packers) as well as by packers.

findings.title: Control Flow Guard is not enabled
evidence: Control Flow Guard (GUARD_CF): GUARD_CF is not set
limitations: Describes how hard the file is to exploit, not whether it is malicious: older toolchains, statically linked and embedded software often lack these mitigations.
CFG is only worthwhile for code built with it; many third-party and non-MSVC toolchains do not offer it.

findings.title: Imports cryptographic APIs
limitations: API presence alone proves nothing: legitimate software (debuggers, installers, security and remote-support tools, games, browsers) imports the same functions.
Cryptography is used for TLS, hashing, licensing and DRM as often as for ransomware or payload decryption; static imports cannot tell which.
Statically linked crypto code (Go, Rust, bundled OpenSSL) leaves no import trace.

No call to these functions was found in the executable sections, so no code is shown: they may be called through pointers or resolved at run time, or the code that uses them may be packed or lie where this scan does not look.

findings.title: Data is appended after the PE image
evidence: overlay of 6.2 KiB (33% of the file)
limitations: Installers, self-extractors, Python/Electron/Go bundlers and signed binaries append data on purpose; malware droppers hide payloads the same way. The overlay is not analysed here.
The Authenticode certificate table is excluded from the overlay size when it sits at the end of the file.

risk.label: critical
basis: points per finding = severity (info 0, low 4, medium 10, high 20, critical 40) x confidence (low 0.4, medium 0.7, high 1.0), rounded

limitations: Static analysis only; the file was never executed.
Findings are leads, not verdicts: each one states its evidence and how it can be wrong, and the risk score only orders a review queue.
Imports resolved at run time, and code hidden by packers or protectors, are invisible to static analysis.
Some very long strings were split into fragments at the scanner's length cap, so they appear as several shorter strings.
